subject: Re: CloudOptic MSA — Governing Law, Venue & Emergency Relief
content:

Subject: CloudOptic MSA redlines — governing law & venue

Camila,

Attached are our latest redlines to the MSA (CloudOptic_MSA_redlines_v3.docx). Two points wed like to highlight up front so we can avoid back-and-forth:

1) Governing law: CloudOptic insists on California law (our HQ state).
2) Venue / injunctive relief: wed prefer exclusive jurisdiction in the federal and state courts sitting in San Francisco for any court actions. For arbitration, wed accept it for monetary disputes but want an express carveout so either party can seek equitable relief in San Francisco courts.

Were trying to keep things simple for procurement and our internal counsel. Happy to jump on a quick call if helpful.

Thanks,
Samir Patel
Head of Procurement
CloudOptic, Inc.

From: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.com>

Date: Tue, 28 Sep 2027 11:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: CloudOptic MSA redlines — governing law & venue

Samir — thank you for the redlines and the callout on those two items. Looping in Olga (legal) and Karthik (sales lead) to align on a practical compromise.

High-level reaction from Redwood:
- Governing law: we prefer Delaware corporate law as standard for our MSA portfolio. Were not dogmatic, but Delaware provides predictability for commercial contract interpretation.
- Venue / injunctive relief: we want arbitration as the primary dispute resolution mechanism (to avoid costly jurisdictional fights) but understand the need for emergency injunctive relief. We typically use a bridge clause that preserves the right to seek interim equitable relief in any court of competent jurisdiction without waiving arbitration.

Proposed path: Olga proposes specific language that narrows the carveout to interim or emergency equitable relief (injunctive/provisional measures) and confirms those proceedings do not waive the requirement to arbitrate the underlying dispute. Well send language and an explanation of trade-offs. If CloudOptic can accept a bridge clause, that should get procurement across the line while keeping arbitration for all other disputes.

Can you confirm whether class-action waiver / representative actions are a concern? That often drives customers toward courts.

Camila Reyes
Senior Accounts Manager | Redwood Inference
camila.reyes@redwood.com

Samir / team — thanks for the redlines. Ive reviewed and here are the legal trade-offs and suggested text. Attaching a short FAQ that explains why we ask for Delaware and how the bridge clause works (Emergency-Relief-FAQ.pdf).

Key points and suggested language (high level):
1) Governing law: Delaware law (excluding choice-of-law rules) provides consistency. If CloudOptic requires California, we can accept California law limited to issues of contract interpretation where it does not conflict with core commercial standards.

Suggested clause: "This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of Delaware, without regard to its conflicts of law principles; provided, however, that if Customer (CloudOptic) requires the law of the State of California, the Parties agree that California law shall apply solely to matters of procedural venue and equitable remedies, but Delaware law shall govern substantive contract claims."

2) Venue & emergency relief: Redwood is comfortable with arbitration (ICC rules; seat: San Francisco) for final resolution of disputes. For urgent equitable relief (injunctive or interim measures) we propose a narrow carveout: either party may seek such relief in any court of competent jurisdiction (including the United States District Court for the Northern District of California) without waiving the agreement to arbitrate the dispute. This preserves speed for urgent preservation remedies while keeping arbitration intact for the merits.

Suggested emergency relief wording: "Notwithstanding the Parties agreement to arbitrate, either Party may seek interim or emergency equitable relief in any court of competent jurisdiction to preserve the status quo, prevent irreparable harm, or secure assets; such request for interim relief shall not constitute a waiver of the Parties agreement to submit the dispute to arbitration."

3) Class actions and consolidation: we will insist on an express class-action / representative-action waiver that applies in arbitration and in court, as permitted by applicable law. If Customer cannot accept a full waiver, we can propose a limited opt-out process.

4) Practical ask: Our contracts team prefers a single enumerated seat (San Francisco) for arbitration administration to simplify logistics. Were open to ICC/AAA but prefer ICC for cross-border enforceability. If CloudOptic prefers AAA (U.S.-centric), we can discuss.

Next steps: Ill attach a clean redline with the bridge clause and the alternate governing-law sentence for CloudOptics counsel to review. Can the CloudOptic legal team confirm whether California law is a hard requirement or an ask driven by internal procurement policy?

Regards,
Olga Petrov
Senior Counsel, Contracts | Redwood Inference
olga.petrov@redwood.com

Attachment: Emergency-Relief-FAQ.pdf (3 pages)

Olga / Camila — thanks for the quick reply and the language. A couple of follow-ups from our side: 

- The California governing-law ask is primarily procurement-driven (internal policy). It is negotiable if we get clear, binding language that emergency injunctive relief can be obtained in San Francisco and that such steps wont prejudice our ability to pursue consequential remedies later.
- Class-action waiver: our general counsel will not accept a complete waiver for consumer-facing claims (CloudOptic has a small subset of end-user contracts). We can accept a waiver for commercial disputes between the parties but need carveouts for consumer/regulatory claims.

Wed prefer a short call to finalize — do you have availability today 11:00 PT? Also: Ive started a DocuSign envelope for other SOW documents (link below), but not for the MSA yet.

Samir
